# Contribution of Key Comorbidities to Unfavorable Treatment Outcomes among Adults with Drug-sensitive Pulmonary Tuberculosis in India: a Prospective Cohort Analysis

**Authors:** Pranay Sinha; Meagan Karoly; Chandrasekaran Padmapriyadarsini; Mandar Paradkar; Vidya Mave; Nikhil Gupte; Amita Gupta; Madolyn Dauphinais; Senbagavalli Prakash Babu; Sanjay Gaikwad; Samyra R. Viswanathan Diabetes Research Centre, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India | 11.Center for Emerging Pathogens, Department of Medicine, New Jersey Medical School, Rutgers Biomedical and Health Sciences, Newark, New Jersey, United States of America | 12.Department of Medicine, UMass Chan Medical School, Worcester, Massachusetts, USA | 13.Department of Epidemiology, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 14.Department of Biostatistics, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 15.Department of Global Health, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

The population-level impact of risk factors for unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes depends on their relative prevalence in the population. We calculated unadjusted and adjusted attributable fractions (AFs) to estimate the proportion of unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes that can be attributed to key risk factors in India.

What proportion of unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes can be attributed to key risk factors in India?

Adults with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis were enrolled from 5 diverse clinical sites at treatment initiation and prospectively evaluated for 24 months. The primary outcome was a composite unfavorable treatment outcome of failure, recurrence, or death. We estimated the unadjusted and adjusted AFs for potentially modifiable risk factors of unfavorable treatment outcomes.

2930 adults contributed 32912 person-months of follow-up. Median age was 43 (IQR 31–52) years, 2136 (72.9%) were male, 1609 (55.5%) were undernourished, 1182 (40.4%) ever-smoked, 956 (32.8%) had diabetes, 437 (14.9%) reported alcohol misuse, and 65 (2.2%) were HIV positive. Overall, 129 failed treatment, 80 had recurrence, and 101 died. In our unadjusted analysis, 32.2% (95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 23.1–40.3) of all unfavorable outcomes were attributable to undernutrition, 19.4% (95%CI 12.3–25.8) were attributable to ever-smoking, 8.5% (95% CI: 4.3–12.6) to alcohol misuse and 1.6% (95%CI 0.1–3.0) to HIV coinfection. After adjusting for simultaneous presence of multiple risk factors, we found 29.0% (95% CI: 17.6–38.8) of all unfavorable outcomes were attributable to undernutrition. Alcohol misuse and ever-smoking accounted for 15.4% (95% CI: 7.9–22.3) and 17.9% (95% CI: 1.1–31.9) of treatment failures.

Undernutrition, ever-smoking, and alcohol misuse accounted for over a third of all unfavorable treatment outcomes and may present high-yield intervention targets to improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes in India.

Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant global health issue, with an estimated 10.6 million individuals worldwide developing tuberculosis disease annually. India bears a disproportionately high burden, accounting for approximately 27% of these cases1. Tuberculosis is the third leading cause of death in India and in 2021, an estimated 311,807 persons with tuberculosis (PWTB) had an unfavorable clinical outcome of treatment failure, recurrence, or death2. Multiple well-established risk factors contribute to the high incidence and poor clinical outcomes of TB, including undernutrition, smoking, alcohol misuse, diabetes, and HIV3–5. Estimating their relative population-level impact is critical to identify and prioritize high-yield interventions to improve clinical outcomes in tuberculosis6.

Attributable fraction (AF) is an epidemiologic measure that estimates the proportion of all cases of a particular disease or outcome in a population that may be attributable to a specific exposure. AFs are widely used to assess the public health impact of risk factors and targeted interventions1,2,6,7. While the AFs of key risk factors for tuberculosis disease incidence are reported annually, a similar approach has yet to be applied to tuberculosis treatment outcomes1. Further, most studies estimating AFs rely on unadjusted AFs calculated using formulas such as Levine’s method8. These unadjusted AFs capture the total contribution of each risk factor to the outcome but do not account for confounding factors or the presence of multiple correlated risk factors. As a result, unadjusted AFs may overestimate or underestimate the true impact of individual risk factors. In contrast, adjusted AFs measure the contribution of each risk factor while accounting for the simultaneous contribution of other key risk factors9.

PWTB often simultaneously express multiple correlated risk-factors (eg: smoking and alcohol misuse). Since interventions typically target a specific risk-factor, estimating the direct impact of reducing the exposure to a given risk-factor, with all other exposures remaining unchanged, is essential for targeting public health interventions. Therefore, we conducted this prospective cohort analysis to estimate both unadjusted and adjusted AFs for unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes that can be attributed to key risk factors in India, with a focus on providing actionable insights for public health interventions10.

## Study Design and Methods

### Study design and setting:

We conducted a prospective cohort study among adults (≥18 years) with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis initiating treatment between 2015 and 2019 as part of the previously described RePORT India Consortium11. We obtained data from 5 epidemiologically and geographically diverse clinical research sites (Byramjee Jeejeebhoy Government Medical College, Pue; Christian Medical College, Vellore; Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, Puducherry; National Institute of Research in Tuberculosis, Chennai; and Prof. M. Viswanathan Diabetes Research Centre, Chennai) across India that followed a harmonized study protocol and data collection instruments. The sites are a mixture of public and private hospitals from western, central, and southern India. All sites cooperated with the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), and recruitment for our study included outpatients in the NTEP program.

We enrolled adults with microbiological evidence of pulmonary tuberculosis based on Xpert MTB/RIF assay or solid/liquid cultures within 7 days of tuberculosis treatment initiation. We excluded those with any molecular or phenotypic resistance to first-line tuberculosis drugs. We prospectively evaluated participants during tuberculosis treatment and for 18 months after treatment completion for unfavorable treatment outcomes of failure, recurrence, or death.

### Exposures:

Our primary exposures included undernutrition, smoking history, alcohol misuse, diabetes, and HIV status at the initiation of tuberculosis treatment. We chose these exposures as they are potentially modifiable risk factors of unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes1,12–15. We relied on self-reporting to assess smoking history (ever or never smoked). We defined ever-smoking as having smoked at least 100 tobacco products during the participant’s lifetime. We defined undernutrition16 as body mass index (BMI) below 18.5 kg/m2. Alcohol misuse was defined as having an Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-c) score ≥4 points for men and ≥3 points for women17. We used a composite of glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) value ≥6.5%, random blood glucose ≥200mg/dL, or prior physician diagnosis to define diabetes18. We confirmed HIV status at treatment initiation by ELISA. We additionally evaluated the duration of symptomatic illness prior to treatment initiation as a marker for delays in diagnosis and/or treatment initiation.

### Outcomes:

The primary outcome was a composite unfavorable treatment outcome of failure, recurrence, or death. We defined failure as having microbiological (smear microscopy or culture) or clinical (signs and/or symptoms) evidence of tuberculosis disease during the final two months of treatment. We defined recurrence as microbiological (smear microscopy or culture) or clinical (signs and/or symptoms) evidence of tuberculosis disease among individuals following successful treatment completion. Death, in our analysis, connotes all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included failure, recurrence, and death which were all analyzed individually.

### Statistical analysis:

Baseline characteristics were described by treatment outcome and compared using t-test for continuous variables and χ2 test for categorical variables. Univariable Cox proportional hazards regression was done to identify variables associated with unfavorable treatment outcomes. Person-time at risk was calculated from the time of treatment initiation to the occurrence of the first mutually exclusive outcome (failure or recurrence or death), loss to follow-up, or until right-censoring at 18 months after treatment completion.

Our primary analysis estimated both unadjusted and adjusted attributable fractions for the composite unfavorable outcome. For unadjusted AFs, we applied the formula: AF = P(HR - 1) / [P(HR - 1) + 1], where P is the prevalence of the exposure and HR is its risk estimate from unadjusted Cox regression8,19 For adjusted AFs, we used the approach proposed by Greenland et al.: AF = (O - E) / O where O represents the observed number of outcomes, and E is the expected number of outcomes in a counterfactual scenario in which the exposure is eliminated while all other variables remain unchanged9. The survival probability for each individual under observed conditions was calculated as: S(t|X) = S0(t) ^ (exp(βX)), where S0(t) is the baseline survival function, X represents the exposure and covariates, and β is the estimated coefficient from the Cox model. For the adjusted analysis, survival probabilities incorporated all covariates: S(t|X) = S0(t) ^ (exp(β1X1 + β2X2 + … + βkXk)). The probability of an event occurring was derived as: P(event) = 1 - S(t|X). E was estimated by summing each participant’s predicted probability of experiencing the outcome under the hypothetical counterfactual scenario in which the exposure of interest was eliminated from the dataset, while all other variables remain unchanged.

Additionally, we conducted four sensitivity analyses:

#### Imputed Person-Time Exclusion:

For a subset of participants (n = 132), follow-up dates beyond enrollment were missing, although treatment outcomes were available. To include these individuals in time-to-event analyses, we assigned imputed person-time values based on the median follow-up durations among participants who died and those lost to follow-up. To evaluate whether this imputation introduced bias, we conducted a sensitivity analysis excluding these individuals and re-estimated both unadjusted and adjusted AFs.

#### HIV Stratified by ART Status:

Given the low prevalence of HIV in our cohort, we conducted a disaggregated analysis stratifying HIV-positive participants by ART status at TB treatment initiation. Untreated HIV was defined as HIV-positive individuals not on ART at baseline, while treated HIV referred to those already on ART. We compared the AFs for these subgroups to determine whether the excess risk of unfavorable outcomes was primarily associated with untreated HIV.

#### Joint Exposure to Smoking and Alcohol Misuse:

To assess potential interaction or synergy between smoking and alcohol misuse, we constructed a joint exposure variable with four categories: neither exposure, smoking only, alcohol misuse only, and both exposures. We estimated hazard ratios and AFs for each category, both in the full cohort and among men only, to evaluate whether the co-occurrence of these behaviors conferred additive or multiplicative risk.

#### Male-Restricted Analysis:

Because men composed the majority of our study population and are disproportionately affected by TB and related behavioral risk factors, we conducted a sex-restricted analysis among male participants. This allowed us to evaluate whether the magnitude and statistical significance of AFs differed in this higher-risk subgroup, particularly for exposures like smoking and alcohol misuse.

The final regression model was selected using a forward stepwise approach, considering all variables with a significant HR (p-value<0.05) in Supplementary Table 1 and clinically relevant risk factors that are epidemiologically important per the WHO1. All adjusted analyses included all exposures (undernutrition, ever-smoking, HIV-positive, alcohol misuse, diabetes, symptom duration), age, and sex of the participant. We conducted all analyses in Stata 1720 (Stata Corp, College Station, TX) and considered p-value <0.05 to be statistically significant.

## Results

### Profile of Study Cohort:

A total of 2,930 adults with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis were enrolled and contributed 32,912 person-months of follow-up. The median duration of follow-up was 10.6 months (IQR 6.8–13.3). Among these, 132 participants (28 deaths, 104 lost to follow-up [LTFU]) lacked follow-up dates beyond enrollment. To retain these participants in time-to-event analyses, we imputed person-time using the median follow-up durations for those who died (2.06 months) and those LTFU (1.73 months).

Overall, 310 participants (10.6%) experienced unfavorable treatment outcomes: 129 (4.4%) failed treatment, 101 (3.4%) died, and 80 (2.7%) experienced recurrence. The cohort was predominantly male (72.9%) with a median age of 43 years (IQR 31–52). At treatment initiation, 1,609 (55.5%) were undernourished, 1,182 (40.4%) reported ever-smoking, 956 (32.8%) had diabetes, 437 (14.9%) reported alcohol misuse, and 65 (2.2%) were HIV positive. Among persons with HIV, 26 (46.4%) were on ART at enrollment (Table 1).

### Unadjusted Attributable Fractions:

In unadjusted models (Table 2), 32.2% (95% CI: 23.1–40.3) of all unfavorable outcomes were attributable to undernutrition. Other exposures with significant AFs included ever-smoking (19.4%, 95% Cl: 12.3–25.8), alcohol misuse (8.5%, 95% Cl: 4.3–12.6), and HIV coinfection (1.6%, 95% Cl: 0.18–3.04). Diabetes and symptom duration prior to treatment initiation were not associated with statistically significant unadjusted AFs. The unadjusted hazard ratios used to derive these estimates are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

When treatment outcomes were disaggregated (Table 3), undernutrition accounted for 40.3% (95% Cl: 24.1–53.1) of deaths, 43.7% (95% Cl: 30.8–54.3) of failures, and 4.8% (95% Cl: −19.2–24.1) of recurrences. Ever-smoking and alcohol misuse contributed substantially to treatment failure (26.6% and 19.3%, respectively), and ever-smoking was also associated with death (24.9%). No statistically significant AFs were found for recurrence across any exposure.

### Adjusted Attributable Fractions:

After adjusting for all exposures, as well as age and sex, undernutrition remained the only factor significantly associated with unfavorable outcomes, accounting for 29.0% (95% Cl: 17.6–38.8) of all events (Table 2). Adjusted AFs for ever-smoking, alcohol misuse, HIV, diabetes, and prolonged symptom duration were not statistically significant.

In disaggregated adjusted analyses (Table 3), undernutrition remained the dominant contributor to both deaths (34.9%, 95% Cl:13.6–50.9) and treatment failures (38.1%, 95% Cl: 20.7–51.6). Alcohol misuse (15.4%, 95% Cl: 7.9–22.3) and ever-smoking (17.9%, 95% Cl: 1.1–31.9) were also significantly associated with treatment failure, but not with death or recurrence. No exposures had statistically significant AFs for recurrence.

### Sensitivity Analyses:

We repeated all AF calculations after excluding the 132 participants with imputed follow-up time. The findings remained consistent with the primary analysis (Supplementary Table 2). In this restricted cohort, undernutrition accounted for 30.6% (95% CI: 20.8–39.1) of unfavorable outcomes, followed by ever-smoking (18.0%, 95% CI: 10.5–24.8), alcohol misuse (9.0%, 95% CI: 4.5–13.3), and HIV (1.9%, 95% CI: 0.5–3.4). In adjusted analyses, undernutrition (27.9%, 95% CI: 16.0–38.2) and HIV (1.7%, 95% CI: 0.02–3.2) remained significantly associated with outcomes; smoking and alcohol misuse did not.

We also evaluated the contribution of HIV by ART status (Supplementary Table 3). Among participants with untreated HIV, 1.9% (95% Cl: 1.2–2.5) of unfavorable outcomes were attributable to HIV, whereas no significant AF was found for those already on ART (adjusted AF: −0.2%, 95% CI: −1.6–1.2). This supports the hypothesis that a lack of ART coverage largely drives the contribution of HIV to poor TB outcomes.

Given their high co-occurrence, we examined the joint effect of smoking and alcohol misuse (Supplementary Tables 4). In unadjusted models, individuals with both exposures had significantly higher hazards of unfavorable outcomes compared to those with neither (HR 1.84, 95% CI: 1.3–2.5). However, these associations attenuated in adjusted models (HR 1.49, 95% CI: 1.05–2.1) in the full population. Among men, the unadjusted HR was 1.48 (98% Cl: 1.02–2.1), and it attenuated to HR 1.27 (95% CI: 0.8–1.8) in the adjusted analysis. No multiplicative interaction was detected. This supports the conclusion that the observed joint effects are likely due to shared confounding rather than synergistic biological interaction.

We conducted a sex-restricted analysis among male participants only (Supplementary Table 5). In unadjusted models, 40.0% (95% Cl: 30.3–48.9) of unfavorable outcomes were attributable to undernutrition, followed by ever-smoking (13.3%, 95% Cl: 1.04–24.1) and alcohol misuse (6.1%, 95% Cl: −0.4–12.1). In adjusted models, undernutrition remained significantly associated with unfavorable outcomes (36.8%, 95% Cl: 24.5–47.1), while AFs for ever-smoking, alcohol misuse, and HIV were not statistically significant.

## Discussion

To our knowledge, this is the first paper to assess AFs for tuberculosis treatment outcomes. Previous work has established the AFs for undernutrition, HIV, smoking, alcohol misuse, and diabetes in driving TB incidence; our findings shed light on their relative contributions to treatment outcomes. In both unadjusted and adjusted analyses, we found undernutrition to be the leading driver of unfavorable TB treatment outcomes in India. HIV had a much lower contribution, in part due to its low prevalence in this population. These data are critical to inform the priorities of India’s National Tuberculosis Elimination Program (NTEP).

In our analysis, approximately one-third of unfavorable outcomes were attributable to undernutrition, largely driven by deaths and treatment failures. Undernutrition is widespread among PWTB, affecting over 50% in this cohort. Nutritional deficiencies impair the immune response to TB, weakens respiratory muscles needed for ventilation, affects pharmacokinetic exposure, and increases toxicity21,22. Of note, our cohort preceded government nutritional support programs for PWTB such as the Nikshay Poshan Yojana and the Nikshay-Mitra program. However, even today many individuals do not receive these interventions during the critical intensive phase of treatment which is the highest risk period for mortality23.

To maximize the impact of nutritional interventions, they should be provided promptly at treatment initiation, particularly to those with severe undernutrition. Mathematical modeling suggests that population-level nutritional interventions, such as one through India’s existing public distribution system, would be highly cost-effective as they would reduce tuberculosis incidence as well as mortality24. Model projections have been corroborated by empirical data in the landmark RATIONS study which showed reduction in TB incidence in Indian households receiving foodbaskets for PWTB and their household contacts25. More recently, a cluster randomized trial in India linked food baskets to improved treatment outcomes26. Our study supports further evidence that nutritional interventions may be a high-yield strategy for improving clinical outcomes in tuberculosis in India.

Whereas HIV coinfection was associated with unfavorable treatment outcomes, its relative contribution was much lower compared to undernutrition and alcohol misuse. Only 2% of all unfavorable outcomes in our study were attributed to HIV. The low prevalence of HIV, which was 2.2% in our study population, likely explains this finding. Notably, our disaggregated analysis showed that the modest contribution of HIV to unfavorable outcomes was largely driven by those not on ART at TB treatment initiation. These findings highlight the importance of ART initiation at TB diagnosis and reinforce the value of integrated HIV-TB services to improve outcomes. Similarly, poor glycemic control is associated with a higher risk of unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes. However, we did not find a significant contribution of diabetes to unfavorable treatment outcomes in our study. Whereas the precise reasons for this are unclear, better care-seeking behaviors, metformin use and relatively higher BMI among diabetic participants may explain some of our findings27–30.

In unadjusted models, smoking and alcohol misuse appeared to have large contributions to unfavorable outcomes. However, they lost statistical significance when we derived adjusted Afs. This illustrates the importance of adjusted attributable fractions, which account for the overlap and co-linearity of exposures. Unadjusted AFs may overestimate the impact of a single exposure when it is correlated with others, whereas adjusted AFs better isolate the direct contribution of each risk factor after controlling for confounding. We did assess for synergy between smoking and alcohol use given their frequent co-occurrence, but did not find this to be the case in the general population or solely among men.

A key strength of our study was the epidemiologically diverse study population from 5 different study sites across India. The relatively large sample size enabled the analysis of each treatment outcome independently and estimated the relative contribution of potentially modifiable risk factors to guide interventions. Further, we present unadjusted and adjusted AFs for unfavorable tuberculosis treatment outcomes to provide unbiased estimates. Lastly, we enrolled PWTB from the public and private sectors collaborating with the Indian National Tuberculosis Elimination Program.

A key limitation of our study was the lack of objective assessment of treatment adherence. However, some of our exposures, such as alcohol misuse, are associated with poor treatment adherence, which may lie on the causal pathway. Further, it is unclear if the recurrences documented in our study are due to relapse or reinfection, which may change the interpretation of our AF estimates related to recurrence. Also, while our analysis considered the presence of diabetes, alcohol misuse, tobacco use, and HIV as binary exposures, we were unable to categorize participants based on the severity of these conditions. Similarly, undernutrition was only defined using BMI which does not discriminate between different body compositions and provides no information on micronutrient deficiencies. Also, alcohol and tobacco use were self-reported, which makes them susceptible to recall bias, particularly among women given prevailing stigma. This limits our ability to fully assess the impact of disease control on tuberculosis treatment outcomes, which could inform more nuanced public health interventions aimed at improving the management of comorbidities during tuberculosis treatment. Finally, our results may not be generalizable to all of India, especially regions with high HIV burden, or to people with either extrapulmonary or drug-resistant manifestations of tuberculosis, both of which were excluded from this analysis.

## Interpretation

In conclusion, undernutrition accounted for over a quarter of all unfavorable treatment outcomes and may present a high-yield intervention target among adults PWTB in India.
